To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the organizational predictors of work-family practices were: organizational size, the age of the workforce, the percentage of female employees, and the organizational track record in human resources management.
The more women there are in the workforce of a particular organization, the more likely it is that that organization will provide a broad array of work-family benefits.

large, public sector organizations with a high percentage of women and an older workforce were more likely to offer work-family practices than smaller, private sector organizations with a lower percentage of women and a younger workforce.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a model of work-family policies that is grounded in the organizational literature and that can be used to guide organizations as they develop their policies.
the provision of organizational work-family practices.
the development and implementation of a strategic approach to work-family practices, which we have termed the work-family strategic approach (WFSA).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

larger organizations are better able than smaller organizations to provide a broader base of work-family practices and that organizations with a high percentage of women are better able to offer a broader range of work-family practices than organizations with a low percentage of women.

larger organizations with a higher percentage of female employees are more likely to provide a broad range of work-family policies and practices than smaller organizations with a smaller percentage of female employees.
the more a company is involved in human resource management the more likely they are to provide work-family benefits.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
work-family practices are not a panacea for all of the problems associated with balancing work and family.
the provision of work‐family benefits and programs by organizations is not a random occurrence.

the organizational predictors of work-family practices are organizational size and the age of the workforce, and that these variables influence the provision of work family practices in different ways.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is an opportunity for companies to do a much better job of supporting their workers’ work-life balance.

the most successful organizations in terms of work-life balance are those with the most progressive policies, and that the best way to get those progressive policies is to have more women in senior leadership positions.
there is no single solution to work-life balance for everyone.
